entries.meaning: In every house people prepared various vehicles, their hearts joyful at the morning departure. Bharata went home and reflected: “The city, horses, elephants, palaces, stores, and every possession belong to Raghupati. If I abandon them and depart without arranging their care, the outcome will not be good for me; I would become the crest-jewel of sinners, a traitor to my master. A true servant acts for the master’s welfare even if someone imputes millions of faults.” With this resolve he summoned upright servants who would not deviate from duty even in a dream. He explained the whole matter and its moral basis, assigning each person according to fitness. After making every arrangement and posting guards, Bharata went to Rāma’s mother. Knowing that all the distressed mothers understood affection, he ordered palanquins and comfortable litters prepared as conveyances for them.

Like separated cakravāka pairs, the city’s women and men longed intensely in their hearts for dawn. Everyone passed the night awake; when morning came, Bharata summoned the discerning ministers and said, “Bring the complete coronation equipment. In the forest we shall give kingship to the sage Rāma.” Hearing “Hurry,” the ministers bowed and rapidly readied horses, chariots, and elephants. The great sage went first upon a chariot with Arundhatī, the sacred fire, and ritual equipment. The company of brahmins, treasuries of austerity and splendor, mounted various vehicles and departed. All the townspeople made ready and set out for Citrakūṭa. The beautiful palanquins cannot be described; the queens mounted them one after another and traveled. Entrusting the city to upright servants and sending everyone respectfully ahead, Bharata and Śatrughna remembered Rāma and Sītā’s feet and then departed.

words.grammar: collective noun coordinated with the sacred fire

entries.meaning: Controlled solely by longing for the sight of Rāma, all the men and women advanced like herds of elephants intent upon water. Remembering that Sītā and Rāma were in the forest, Bharata and his younger brother traveled on foot. Seeing their love, the people became devoted too, dismounted, and left horses, elephants, and chariots behind. Drawing her litter near, Rāma’s mother spoke gently: “Son, for your mother’s sake mount the chariot; otherwise the beloved family will suffer. When you walk, everyone else walks, yet all are emaciated by grief and unfit for the road.” Placing her words upon his head and bowing at her feet, both brothers mounted the chariot. They spent the first day by the Tamasā and the second on the Gomatī’s bank. For Rāma’s sake people observed disciplines and vows, abandoning ornaments and pleasures: some lived on milk, some on fruit, some ate only one night, and some took one meal.

After staying on the Sai’s bank, they departed at dawn and all drew near Śṛṅgaverapura. Niṣāda king Guha heard every report and sorrowfully reflected: “Why is Bharata going to the forest? Is there some deception in his heart? If there were no inward crookedness, why bring an army? He thinks he will kill Rāma with his younger brother and rule an unchallenged, pleasant kingdom. Bharata did not take sound statecraft to heart; that was a stain, but now life itself is at risk. Even if every god and demon assembled to fight, none could conquer Rāma in battle. Yet why wonder if Bharata acts so? A poisonous vine does not bear nectar-fruit.” Thinking thus, Guha told his kinsmen to be fully alert: “Seize what is at hand, sink the boats, and fortify the landing places.”

“Be fully equipped, block the landing, and form every battle formation fit for men resolved to die. I shall meet Bharata steel to steel and will not let him cross the Gaṅgā alive. Death in battle on Gaṅgā’s bank, in Rāma’s cause, with this momentary body! Bharata is the king and Rāma’s brother, while I am a low-born servant; only through immense fortune is such a death obtained. I shall fight fiercely for my master’s cause and whiten my fame through all fourteen worlds. I shall give up life for Raghunātha’s sake: for me each hand holds a sweetmeat of joy. One who has no standing in holy society and not even a line among Rāma’s devotees lives upon the earth only as a burden, an axe to the tree of the mother’s youth.” Free of dejection, the Niṣāda chief raised everyone’s ardor, remembered Rāma, and immediately called for quiver, bow, and armor.

words.grammar: noun in an idiom of obtaining a benefit in both hands

entries.meaning: “Hurry, brothers—arm and equip yourselves!” Hearing the king’s order, no one quailed. “Very well, lord,” all replied joyfully, each spurring the next into zeal. The Niṣāda warriors came forward and repeatedly saluted; every hero relished the battle’s fierce contest. Remembering Rāma’s lotus feet and taking their vow, they tied on quivers and strung their bows. They put on finger guards and headgear and readied axes, bamboo staves, and arrows. Some, highly skilled in wielding swords, leapt into the air as though leaving the earth. Once each company had prepared its own equipment, they came and saluted King Guha. Seeing that all the fighters were capable, he honored each by name. “Brothers, do not betray me today; a great task confronts me.” Hearing this, the valiant warriors answered indignantly, “Do not be anxious.”

The warriors said: “Through Rāma’s majesty and your strength, lord, we could destroy the army even without warriors or horses. While alive we shall not step backward; we shall cover the earth with headless trunks and severed heads.” Seeing a fine force, the Niṣāda lord ordered the war drum sounded. As he spoke, a sneeze came from the left, and omen-readers said the field was favorable. An elder considered the sign and said, “You will meet Bharata, but there will be no battle. Bharata is going to appease Rāma; the omen says there is no conflict.” Guha answered, “The elder speaks well. Fools who act rashly repent. Without understanding Bharata’s disposition and character, it would be a great loss to a friend to fight without knowing.” He ordered the warriors assembled at the landing: “I shall meet him and learn the secret. Having discerned the stance between friend and enemy, I will return and act accordingly.”

Guha knew that Lakṣmaṇa’s naturally lovely affection could not conceal either enmity or love, however hidden. Having said this, he began to prepare a meeting gift and called for tubers, roots, fruits, birds, game, and loads of plump, mature pāṭhīna fish, which bearers brought in abundance. With the meeting gifts prepared, he set out to meet Bharata and received auspicious signs, roots of blessing. From a distance he announced his own name and prostrated before the lord of sages. Knowing him to be dear to Rāma, the sage blessed him and told Bharata clearly who he was. Hearing “Rāma’s friend,” Bharata abandoned his chariot, climbed down, and hurried forward as love surged within him. Guha announced his village, community, and name; Bharata placed his forehead upon the ground in salutation. Seeing him prostrate, Bharata clasped him to his heart as though meeting Lakṣmaṇa, and the love within could not be contained.

words.grammar: fish name in an offering list

entries.meaning: Bharata met Guha with deepest affection, and people marveled at love’s way. The cry “Blessed! Blessed!” arose, the root of blessing; the gods praised them and showered flowers. In worldly and Vedic convention Guha was low in every way, such that ritual sprinkling was taken after touching his shadow; yet Rāma’s younger brother filled his embrace with him, and his body overflowed with thrills. Those who merely yawn while saying “Rāma, Rāma” are not approached by accumulated sins, while Rāma had drawn this man to his heart and purified the world together with his lineage. When the Karmanāśā’s water enters the Gaṅgā, tell me who would not carry it upon the head? The world knows that by repeating the Name in reverse, Vālmīki became like Brahman. Dog-cook, Śabara, Khasa, Yavana, dullard, outcaste, Kol, or Kirāta—by saying “Rāma,” one becomes supremely pure and renowned through the worlds.

There is no wonder in this; it has continued age after age—whom has Raghubīra not ennobled? The gods proclaim the greatness of Rāma’s Name, and Ayodhyā’s people rejoiced to hear it. Meeting Rāma’s friend with love, Bharata asked after his welfare, prosperity, and peace. Seeing Bharata’s character and affection, the Niṣāda at that moment lost awareness of the body. Reserve, love, and joy swelled in his mind; he stood gazing fixedly at Bharata. Recovering composure, he bowed again at Bharata’s feet and petitioned with joined hands and love: “Having seen the lotus feet that are the root of welfare, I count myself fortunate in past, present, and future. Now by your supreme favor, lord, blessing has come to me together with millions of generations. When one considers my conduct and lineage alongside the Lord’s glory, whoever does not worship Raghubīra’s feet has surely been cheated by Fate.”
